summary: Defines an SMTP extension that lets a client name the responsible submitter of a message, meaning the address of the entity that most recently introduced it into the mail stream. Receiving servers can use that to decide whether the client may send for that domain. It was experimental and is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4405 adds one parameter to the SMTP MAIL command. The sending server names the party that most recently put the message into the mail system, so the receiving server can check that claim against the message headers and decide whether the sender was entitled to send on that domain's behalf.

questions: what is the purported responsible domain
subtitle: An SMTP extension that names the party most recently responsible for putting a message into the mail system.

tldr.problem: Senders of unwanted mail routinely pretend to be someone else, and a receiving server had no quick way to tell whether the machine in front of it was allowed to send on behalf of the domain named in the message.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds a SUBMITTER keyword to the EHLO response and a SUBMITTER parameter to the SMTP MAIL command, carrying the address of the entity most recently responsible for introducing the message into the transport stream.
tldr.outcome: A receiving server can check the claim before the message body is sent, and can compare it with the address derived from the message headers. The memo is Experimental, the RFC Editor index lists its status as Historic, and no later RFC obsoletes it.

today: RFC 4405 is an April 2006 Experimental memo published alongside RFC 4406, RFC 4407 and RFC 4408 to document two approaches the MARID working group could not reconcile, and the RFC Editor index lists its status as Historic. No later RFC obsoletes it, so it is kept here as a record of the Responsible Submitter extension.

sections.title: Why the Responsible Submitter Needed Naming
sections.content:
The practice of falsifying the identity of the sender of an e-mail message, commonly called spoofing, is a prevalent tactic used by senders of unsolicited commercial e-mail, and it has highlighted the need to improve identification of the responsible submitter of a message. In this specification, the responsible submitter is the entity most recently responsible for injecting a message into the e-mail transport stream. The e-mail address of the responsible submitter is the Purported Responsible Address of the message, and the domain portion of that address is the Purported Responsible Domain.

Broadly speaking, there are two possible approaches for determining the purported responsible address: from protocol data, or from message headers. Deriving it from protocol data has the advantage that validation can be performed before the client has transmitted the message body, so a server that detects spoofing can reject the message before it is ever transmitted. Its disadvantage is the risk of false positives, because there are legitimate reasons why the domain names used in SMTP commands may differ from those of the sender of a message.

Deriving the address from message headers has the advantage that validation is usually based on an identity that existing mail user agents display to recipients as the sender's identity, which helps to detect phishing, where a malicious sender tries to fool a recipient into believing a message comes from a well known entity. It carries a lower risk of false positives, since there are fewer legitimate reasons for headers to differ from the true sender. Its disadvantage is that it requires parsing and analysing message headers, and in practice much or all of the message body is also transmitted, because SMTP provides no mechanism to interrupt transmission after the DATA command has been issued.

The RFC describes an approach that unifies the two, using the SMTP extension mechanism to carry the address of the entity most recently responsible for submitting the message, so that a server can validate that the client is authorized to transmit mail on behalf of the responsible submitter's domain.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two ways to work out who is really behind a message: look at what the sending server said, or look at the headers inside the message. The first lets a server stop a message early, the second matches what the reader sees. This RFC combines them.

sections.title: The SUBMITTER Service Extension
sections.content:
The extension is defined in six parts. Its name is Responsible Submitter. The EHLO keyword value associated with it is SUBMITTER. The SUBMITTER keyword has no parameters. No additional SMTP verbs are defined by the extension. An optional parameter is added to the MAIL command using the esmtp-keyword SUBMITTER, and it is used to specify the e-mail address of the entity responsible for submitting the message for delivery. The extension is appropriate for the message submission protocol.

An SMTP server includes the SUBMITTER keyword in its EHLO response to tell the client that the extension is supported. The syntax of the SUBMITTER parameter is SUBMITTER= Mailbox, where Mailbox is the Augmented Backus-Naur Form production defined in section 4.1.2 of the SMTP specification. Characters such as space, plus and equals sign that may occur in Mailbox but are not permitted in ESMTP parameter values must be encoded as xtext, as described in the delivery status notification extension.
sections.plainLanguage: The server says it supports the extension by listing SUBMITTER in its greeting. After that, the client can add a SUBMITTER parameter to the MAIL command, and the value is a normal mail address.

sections.title: Setting and Processing the SUBMITTER Parameter
sections.content:
The purpose of the parameter is to let the client tell the server the purported responsible address of the message directly in the SMTP protocol. Clients that support the extension must include the SUBMITTER parameter on all messages, including messages that contain a null reverse-path in the MAIL command, and must set its value to the purported responsible address of the message. In some circumstances clients may need to add message headers to the message so that the correct SUBMITTER value can be set.

A receiver should select the domain part of the SUBMITTER address as the purported responsible domain, and should perform the tests it considers necessary to determine whether the connecting client is authorized to transmit messages on behalf of that domain. If those tests say the client is not authorized, the server should reject the message and must use the reply 550 5.7.1 Submitter not allowed. If the server allows the client to transmit message data, it should then determine the purported responsible address by examining the message headers as described in the Purported Responsible Address specification, and if that address does not match the address in the SUBMITTER parameter, it must reject the message with the reply 550 5.7.1 Submitter does not match header. If no purported responsible address is found, the server should reject the message with the reply 554 5.7.7 Cannot verify submitter address.

Verifying mail transfer agents are strongly urged to validate the SUBMITTER parameter against the message headers, because otherwise an attacker can trivially defeat the algorithm. The presence of the parameter must not change the effective reverse-path of a message, so delivery status notifications are still sent to the reverse-path, and are not sent to the SUBMITTER address when the reverse-path is null. The parameter must not change the effective reply address either, so replies still go to the From address or the Reply-To address.

When a mail transfer agent forwards a message to another server that does not support the extension, it must transmit the message without the SUBMITTER parameter, which should involve no information loss, since the parameter is required to contain information derived from the message headers.
sections.plainLanguage: The sending server has to fill the parameter in, and the receiving server has to check it twice: once against its own rules about who may send for that domain, and once against the address found in the message headers. A mismatch is a rejected message, and the RFC gives the exact reply text for each case.

sections.title: How SUBMITTER Is Used
sections.content:
The RFC works through five situations. In ordinary mail submission, a mail user agent hands the message to a submission server without the SUBMITTER parameter, the submission server validates the client through some external scheme such as SMTP authentication, and the server then extracts the name from the message headers for use in the SUBMITTER parameter of subsequent transmissions.

For mail forwarding, when Alice sends a message to Bob at his university account, the university server forwards it to Bob's office account. Although the original sender is Alice, she is not responsible for this most recent retransmission, so the forwarding server determines a new purported responsible address, namely Bob's university address, and sets the SUBMITTER parameter accordingly. The forwarding server also inserts a Resent-From header so that the address derived from the headers matches the SUBMITTER address.

For a mobile user, the message travels through the carrier's network but Alice uses her own address on the From line, so that replies go to her office mailbox. The carrier's server uses the SUBMITTER parameter to designate Alice's carrier address as the responsible submitter and also inserts a Sender header so that the address derived from the headers matches. A conventional internet service provider may do the same, designating the user's address on the provider's network if it differs from the MAIL FROM address, which is useful for providers that host several domains or share mail transfer agents among them.

For a guest e-mail service, the hotel routes all outbound mail through its own server and designates a generic account, guest.services at the hotel's domain, as the responsible submitter, because Alice has no account there. It too inserts a Resent-From header. For a non-delivery report, a client sends a message with a null reverse-path but with a SUBMITTER parameter naming a mailer-daemon account, so the report can still be traced.
sections.plainLanguage: Every time a message is passed on, the party that passed it on becomes the responsible submitter, not the person who wrote it. A forwarding server, a mobile carrier and a hotel mail server all set the parameter to their own address and add a header to match.

sections.title: What the Extension Does Not Prove
sections.content:
The extension is an optimization that lets a client identify the responsible submitter in the SMTP protocol, so that servers can validate the identity efficiently before the message contents are transmitted.

It is quite possible for an attacker to forge the value of the SUBMITTER parameter, and it is possible for an attacker to transmit a message whose SUBMITTER parameter does not match the purported responsible address derived from the message headers. The presence of the parameter therefore provides, by itself, no assurance of the authenticity of the message or of the responsible submitter. Rather, it is intended to give receiving systems additional information that lets them determine the validity of the responsible submitter, and specifically whether the client is authorized to transmit mail on behalf of that submitter's domain.

The memo was published together with RFC 4406, RFC 4407 and RFC 4408 as Experimental documents, because there was no general technical consensus and efforts to reconcile the two approaches had failed. The IESG took no position on which approach is to be preferred, cautioned that there are serious open issues for each approach and concerns about using them in tandem, and considered that documenting the different approaches does less harm than not documenting them. It also warned that the way Resent- header fields are used would result in failure to receive legitimate mail when interacting with standards-compliant systems, and that it would be inappropriate to advance the approach on the standards track without resolving that interoperability problem.
sections.plainLanguage: The parameter is a claim, not a proof. Anyone can put a false address in it, which is why the receiving server has to compare it with the headers in the message. The IESG published the memo to record the approach, not to endorse it.

viz.caption: AN SMTP SESSION THAT USES THE SUBMITTER PARAMETER

messages.label: EHLO example.com
messages.note: The client names its own domain.

messages.label: 250 ... SUBMITTER
messages.note: The server lists the extensions it supports, including SUBMITTER.

messages.label: MAIL FROM: alice@example.com SUBMITTER=alice@example.com
messages.note: The client names the party responsible for submitting the message.

messages.label: DATA
messages.note: The client sends the message body.
